summary: Describes conventions for using the Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) and the SKIPJACK encryption algorithm with the enveloped-data and encrypted-data content types of the Cryptographic Message Syntax. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to lock a message with two particular U.S. government-designed locking recipes, inside a standard message wrapper.

subtitle: Conventions for using two government-designed cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

tldr.problem: Developers need standardized conventions for using the Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) and SKIPJACK encryption with CMS to ensure interoperable implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies how to encrypt content using SKIPJACK in 64-bit CBC mode with 8-byte IVs and 80-bit keys, how to wrap content-encryption keys using KEA-generated key-encryption keys, and when to use key agreement versus pre-distributed symmetric keys.
tldr.outcome: Compliant implementations can encrypt and decrypt CMS enveloped-data and encrypted-data content types using KEA and SKIPJACK in a standardized, interoperable way.

today: RFC 2876 is an Informational memo specifying conventions for using KEA and SKIPJACK encryption algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). It defines how to encrypt content, wrap keys, and manage recipients in enveloped-data and encrypted-data messages.

sections.title: Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) and SKIPJACK overview
sections.content:
This RFC describes conventions for using KEA (Key Exchange Algorithm) and SKIPJACK in conjunction with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) enveloped-data and encrypted-data content types. Both are algorithms developed by the U.S. government. SKIPJACK is a symmetric-key block cipher (encryption algorithm), and KEA is used for key agreement—generating a shared encryption key from the two parties' key material.

The RFC applies the key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and MAY as defined in RFC 2119. Software claiming compliance must provide the capabilities indicated by these keywords. KEA and SKIPJACK are described in detail in external specifications; this RFC focuses on how to use them within the CMS framework.
sections.plainLanguage: KEA is like a way two people can agree on a secret number so only they know it. SKIPJACK is a recipe for locking messages. This RFC says exactly how to use both together with a standard message format so everyone does it the same way.

sections.title: Content encryption and decryption process
sections.content:
Content is encrypted using SKIPJACK in 64-bit Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode. The input is padded to a multiple of eight octets according to CMS Section 6.3 rules. Each encryption uses a randomly-generated 8-byte Initialization Vector (IV) and an 80-bit SKIPJACK content-encryption key (CEK).

During decryption, the encryptedContent is decrypted as a single string using the same SKIPJACK algorithm in 64-bit CBC mode, using the 80-bit CEK and 8-byte IV as inputs. After decryption, the padding is removed following the same CMS rules.

For each instance of an enveloped-data content type, the IV and CEK must be randomly generated and the CEK must only be used for that single instance. This ensures that even if two messages are otherwise identical, their encrypted forms will differ because the IV differs.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is split into 8-byte chunks. Each chunk is locked with SKIPJACK using a 80-bit key and an 8-byte random starting number. When unlocking, both the key and random number are needed, and they are used in a specific order (CBC mode).

sections.title: Key management with enveloped-data
sections.content:
The CMS enveloped-data content type wraps encrypted content together with wrapped content-encryption keys for one or more recipients. Two key management techniques are supported: key agreement and previously distributed symmetric keys. The key transport technique MUST NOT be used with KEA.

With key agreement, the SKIPJACK CEK is uniquely wrapped for each recipient using a pairwise symmetric key-encryption key (KEK) generated using KEA, the originator's private KEA key, the recipient's public KEA key, and the originator's User Keying Material (UKM, a 128-byte random value). The RFC defines two options: the originator can use a single shared UKM for all recipients sharing the same KEA parameters (saving space), or a unique UKM for each recipient (more flexible but larger).

With previously distributed symmetric keys, the SKIPJACK CEK is wrapped using a KEK that was distributed outside the CMS mechanism (such as through a key management system). The methods for generating and distributing the symmetric KEK are beyond the scope of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways to send a message: (1) Ask the recipient "What is your public key?" and use that plus a random number to create a unique key just for locking the message for them. (2) Assume you already have a shared secret key with them and just use that. Both work; it depends on the situation.

sections.title: Field requirements and security notes
sections.content:
The EnvelopedData version MUST be 2. If key agreement is used, the originatorInfo field SHOULD include the originator's KEA X.509 v3 certificate containing the public key used to generate each pairwise KEK. The encryptedContentInfo field MUST specify the id-fortezzaConfidentialityAlgorithm OID and MUST include the 8-byte IV in the parameters.

For key agreement, the KeyAgreementRecipientInfo originator field MUST identify the originator via issuerAndSerialNumber or subjectKeyIdentifier (or originatorKey for internal storage scenarios). The keyEncryptionAlgorithm MUST be id-kEAKeyEncryptionAlgorithm and the wrap algorithm MUST be id-fortezzaWrap80, which adds an integrity check and produces a 96-bit output from an 80-bit key.

The FORTEZZA 80-bit wrap function itself is not publicly documented. The RFC provides hexadecimal encodings of the SMIMECapabilities for KEA and SKIPJACK to help implementations announce their capabilities in S/MIME signedData objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The exact format and fields required are specified precisely so different systems will agree. If you say you support this, you promise to follow these rules. The lock procedure adds an extra number to check that the message was not damaged.
